newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong protest ship nears disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong protest ship nears disputed isles.

text.p: A Hong Kong protest ship was steaming towards disputed East China Sea islands where activists planned to demolish a Japanese-built lighthouse, reporters on board were quoted as saying on Wednesday.
The rusty tanker Kien Hwa 2 carrying 18 Hong Kong anti-Japan activists was due to arrive at the islands at around 1430 GMT, Hong Kong government radio quoted correspondents on board as saying.

The 18 activists had vowed to reclaim the islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japanese as the Senkakus, by removing the lighthouse and by raising a People's Republic of China red flag, the radio said.
The protest ship set sail from Hong Kong on Sunday and has continued its course despite bad weather and mounting tension in the region over the dispute.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, returns to Chinese rule next year.

The islands have been the focus of intense anti-Japanese protests by Chinese communities across East Asia and North America since a Japanese right-wing youth group erected the lighthouse and a war memorial on the islands in July.

On Monday five vessels carrying about 20 protesters from Taiwan and Hong Kong and up to 60 journalists tried to land on the islands to tear down the lighthouse, but were repulsed by 17 Japanese patrol ships backed by a helicopter.
A Japanese coastguard spokesman said at least 13 Taiwan ships had tried and failed to get near the islands this month.
Hong Kong's chief civil servant, Anson Chan, fuelled the controversy by referring to the islands by their Japanese name during a visit to Australia.

Shocked legislators in the colony called on Chan, the chief secretary, to explain herself. "I will demand an explanation from her in the coming session of the Legislative Council," said pro-China legislator Cheung Hon-chung.
China accuses Japan of occupying the islands and demands a withdrawal. In Hong Kong three quarters of a million people have signed petitions over the past month urging Japan to get out.
The Hong Kong activists who failed to land on the isles on Monday said they would make a second try next month.
"Our aim is to land on the Diaoyus and remove the lighthouse built by the Japanese youth group and other symbols but we will proceed on a peaceful basis," group spokesman Au Pak-kuen said.
Up to 100 activists have signed up to join the October trip, which would be led by Hong Kong Democratic Party legislator Tsang Kin-shing, Au said.

The Kien Hwa 2's skipper, Ngai Lup-chee, created confusion in Hong Kong, Taiwan and China, on Tuesday when he said he had heard that Japan would stage a live-fire naval drill on the tanker's planned route.
Japanese defence forces denied they had any such plan.
Tokyo's sovereignty claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
